performers: Curtis String Quartet: Jascha Brodsky, violin I; Charles Jaffe, violin II; Max Aronoff, viola; Orlando Cole, cello
intro: The Curtis String Quartet recorded Smetana’s String Quartet No. 1 in E minor, “From My Life”, in New York in March 1940, and Columbia issued it on seven 78-rpm sides. Smetana described the four movements as episodes from his life, and the finale contains a high note representing the whistling in his ears.

sections.label: A · First movement, Allegro vivo appassionato
Coda · Held E to the end

cues.title: Opening chord and viola theme
cues.text: All four instruments open with a chord marked sff. The violins then repeat quavers over a long note in the cello, and the viola enters on the last beat of bar 4 with the first theme, marked sf espress. in bar 5.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg miniature score, p. 1, bars 1–5: sff chord for the four instruments, repeated quavers in the violins over the cello’s tied E, viola upbeat in bar 4 and sf espress. in bar 5. https://archive.org/details/quartetstringsem0000unse
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Josef Srb-Debrnov, 1878
cues.text: Smetana described the first movement as love of music in his youth, with a longing he could not put into words and a premonition of future misfortune.
cues.evidence: Smetana to Josef Srb-Debrnov, 12 April 1878, in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 69; the date of the letter is given in the German preface of the Eulenburg score. Translated from the German text. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

cues.title: Columbia set M-405, 1940
cues.text: Columbia issued this recording as set M-405; its catalogue of October 1940 lists the set at eight sides. The quartet fills seven sides, with the first movement on sides 1 and 2. A side of the scherzo from Tchaikovsky’s Third Quartet completes the set.
cues.evidence: Columbia Catalog, October 1940, Internet Archive item columbia-catalog-october-1940: Smetana, Quartet No. 1 in E Minor, Curtis String Quartet, 8 pts., set M-405. Description of the Internet Archive item mm-405-smetana-sq-1: recorded 6 March 1940, issued May 1940, the side list, and side 8 carrying the Tchaikovsky scherzo. https://archive.org/details/mm-405-smetana-sq-1

cues.title: Second movement, alla Polka
cues.text: The second movement is marked Allegro moderato alla Polka. Smetana wrote that it recalled the cheerful years of his youth, when he composed dances and was known as a passionate dancer.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg miniature score, preface and movement list: II. Allegro moderato alla Polka. Smetana to Srb, 12 April 1878, in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 69. https://archive.org/details/quartetstringsem0000unse
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Meno vivo in D♭ major
cues.text: The middle section of the polka, marked Meno vivo, is in D♭ major. Smetana wrote that the players said they could not get the chords in tune. He added easier alternatives in small notes for the violins and viola.
cues.evidence: Smetana to Srb, 12 April 1878, in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), pp. 69–70: Meno vivo in D♭ major, the players’ objection, and the più facile alternatives for violin I, violin II and viola. Smetana to Urbánek, 21 July 1879, in the preface of the Eulenburg score: “trio des dur”. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third movement, Largo sostenuto
cues.text: In a letter to Srb of 12 April 1878, Smetana wrote that the third movement, Largo sostenuto, recalls the happiness of his first love, the girl who later became his wife.
cues.evidence: Smetana to Srb, 12 April 1878, in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 70; Eulenburg miniature score, movement list: III. Largo sostenuto. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performances
cues.text: Dvořák played the viola at a private performance in April 1878. The first public performance was at the Konvikt in Prague on 29 March 1879, played by Ferdinand Lachner, Jan Pelikán, Josef Krehan and Alois Neruda.
cues.evidence: Dvořák timeline, antonin-dvorak.cz, April 1878: he takes part in the first (private) performance of the quartet, on viola, https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/life/important-dates-in-the-life-of-antonin-dvorak/. Bedřich Smetana Museum catalogue, String Quartet in E minor: 29 March 1879, Prague, Konvikt, with the four players named. https://bedrichsmetana.nm.cz/en/work/detail/string-quartet-in-e-minor/126

cues.title: Letter from Liszt, 1880
cues.text: On 5 May 1880 Liszt wrote to Smetana from Weimar. He praised Má vlast and the overture to Libuše, and asked for the parts of the quartet.
cues.evidence: Liszt to Smetana, Weimar, 5 May 1880, in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 57. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

cues.title: Finale, Vivace
cues.text: Smetana described the finale as the discovery of national music and his joy at success on that path. This is broken off by the high note that marks the onset of his deafness. In his account, a small hope follows, and then a painful memory of his first years.
cues.evidence: Smetana to Srb, 12 April 1878, in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 70; Eulenburg miniature score, movement list: IV. Vivace. Translated from the German text. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Held high E, first violin
cues.text: The running figures stop, and the first violin holds a high E, written under an 8va line, above sustained chords in the other three instruments. In his letter to his publisher of 21 July 1879, Smetana described it as the high whistling that announced his deafness.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg miniature score, p. 45, the section marked Meno presto (bars 222–230): violin I holds E under an 8va line while violin II, viola and cello sustain chords. Smetana to Urbánek, 21 July 1879, printed in the score’s preface: in the finale fate announces the catastrophe of his deafness with a high whistling, the four-line E. https://archive.org/details/quartetstringsem0000unse
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing tempo changes and final chords
cues.text: After the held E the score marks Moderato, then Allegro, then a closing Meno marked p dolce. The last chords are pizzicato and pp.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg miniature score, pp. 46–47: Moderato (dolcissimo), Allegro, Meno (p dolce); the last system carries pizz. and pp. https://archive.org/details/quartetstringsem0000unse
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Jascha Brodsky (violin I), Charles Jaffe (violin II), Max Aronoff (viola), Orlando Cole (cello)
fields.note: The Internet Archive description credits the Curtis String Quartet with these four players and assigns Brodsky to violin I and Jaffe to violin II. The label of side 1 (MM-405 pressing, 70344-D) names Brodsky and Jaffe as violins, Aronoff as viola and Cole as cello, without assigning the violin parts.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: The complete quartet, four movements on seven sides
fields.note: The item lists the movements and parts side by side; the edition used by the players is not identified.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description gives 6 March 1940. No second source for the date was found.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: M-405 (69849-D to 69852-D); automatic sequence AM-405 (69853-D to 69856-D); later reissue MM-405 (70344-D to 70347-D)
fields.note: The label scanned in the item reads MM 405-1, 70344-D, the drop-automatic reissue pressing. The item description says the set was issued in May 1940; Columbia’s October 1940 catalogue lists all three number ranges.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Sides 1–7, matrices XCO 27013 to 27019; side 8, XCO 27020, is Tchaikovsky’s scherzo and is not part of this recording
fields.note: Side 1: first movement, part 1; side 2: first movement, part 2; side 3: second movement, part 1; side 4: second movement, part 2 and third movement, part 1; side 5: third movement, part 2; side 6: third movement, part 3 and finale, part 1; side 7: finale, part 2. Take numbers are not given.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No personal mastering credit is given.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was added to the Internet Archive on 4 July 2022; the date of the transfer is not stated.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Equipment, equalisation and restoration are not stated. The file is a single continuous MP3 of the seven sides.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Smetana died on 12 May 1884; the composition is in the public domain.
fields.note: The death date is from the Bedřich Smetana Museum. This does not cover a later edition or arrangement.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: first issued in 1940, before 1963
fields.note: The project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule applies to a Columbia set issued in 1940: the former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2011 extension applied on 1 November 2013. The Internet Archive description gives the issue as May 1940. Columbia’s own October 1940 catalogue independently lists the set as M-405 (69849-D to 69852-D), so the first issue was no later than October 1940. This is not US or worldwide clearance and not a Creative Commons licence.

composer.epithet: Czech composer and conductor from Litomyšl, whose operas for Prague’s Provisional Theatre include The Bartered Bride; deaf from 1874, he then wrote Má vlast and the quartet From My Life.
facts: Prague from 1843, with the blind teacher Josef Proksch; corresponded with Liszt from 1848 and visited him at Weimar in 1857

Music teacher to Count Thun, 1844–47 · own music institute, Prague, from 1848 · Harmoniska Sällskapet, Gothenburg, 1856–61 · opera of the Provisional Theatre, Prague, from 1866 until deafness ended his conducting in 1874
Letter to Liszt 1848 · Gothenburg 1856 · The Bartered Bride 1866 · deafness 1874 · Jabkenice 1875 · Má vlast complete 1882
Eight completed operas, the six symphonic poems of Má vlast, two string quartets, a piano trio, piano polkas and choruses

quote.text: I wanted to depict the course of my life in tones.
quote.source: Smetana to Josef Srb-Debrnov, 12 April 1878, on the String Quartet No. 1; translated from the German text printed in Bronislav Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895)

composer.background:
Bedřich Smetana was born on 2 March 1824 in the castle brewery at Litomyšl, where his father František was a master brewer. He was the first son after six daughters. At five he played first violin in a quartet on his father’s name day, and on 4 October 1830 he played the piano at an academy given for the emperor’s name day. He was schooled in German, at Jindřichův Hradec, Jihlava, Německý Brod, Prague and, from 1840, Plzeň. Because his schoolwork was suffering, his father put him there under the supervision of a cousin, Josef Franz Smetana, a gymnasium teacher.

In 1843 the cousin persuaded his father to send him to Prague to train as a musician. His parents had become poor and sent no money; the Kolář family took him in, and the blind composer Josef Proksch accepted him as a pupil. In 1844 he became music teacher to Count Leopold Thun, on the recommendation of Friedrich Kittl, director of the Conservatory, and until 1847 he spent much of each year at the Thun castles at Poběžovice and Nové Benátky.
